by: converted (convert1d) from fact_check__1.json and the research's 4 searches

checks.claim: A common passenger elevator rating is 1,000 kg, about 13 people (other common ratings are 630 kg and 800 kg).
checks.why: Sources list 1,000 kg/13 persons as a standard rating, but it is one common rating rather than the single typical one; 630 and 800 kg are also common. The person count comes from a floor-area table (about 75 kg per person).

sources.title: Mastering Passenger Elevator Dimensions: Your Ultimate Guide

checks.claim: A counterweight usually weighs as much as the car plus about 40 to 50 percent of its rated load
checks.why: The elevator.tr glossary gives car tare weight plus 40-50% of rated load. Elevator World confirms 50% was common practice and 40% was used in some cases.

checks.claim: At the 1854 New York Crystal Palace exhibition, Elisha Otis rode a platform up high and had the hoisting rope cut, and his safety catch held the platform.
checks.why: Sources differ on whether Otis cut the rope himself or ordered it cut; Britannica says he ordered it cut, while the 1854 account has him doing it. The venue was the Crystal Palace exhibition, usually called the New York World's Fair.

sources.title: Exhibition of the Industry of All Nations

checks.claim: Traction elevators hang from several steel ropes, usually four to eight (never fewer than three on modern passenger lifts), and a single rope may be strong enough to hold the car alone.
checks.why: Walker Consultants says modern passenger traction elevators have at least three ropes, most use four to eight, and a single rope may be strong enough depending on size. 'Each rope alone' is firmer than the engineering source supports.
